title: Reservoir sliding-window allocation and fragmentation harmonization for KV cache
creator: Amelia Park
description: Design and implement a reservoir-based sliding-window allocation strategy for the KV cache to reduce cross-slab fragmentation and improve GPU memory utilization while preserving low-latency continuous batching behavior.
background: Our current KV cache allocation uses a mix of fixed-size slabs and opportunistic coalescing. Under production traffic patterns with heavy continuous batching and variable sequence lengths we see growing fragmentation (both internal and external) across GPU memory, leading to degraded reservation headroom and higher OOM-induced tail latency. Existing defrag/compaction approaches are either too blocking or too costly in terms of memory churn for real-time inference workloads.
proposed_solution: Introduce a 'reservoir sliding-window' allocator layered on top of the slab pools: 1) allocate from a small hot-window that favors co-located KV entries for active prefixes; 2) maintain a cold reservoir of reclaimed micro-segments that can be stitched to form larger contiguous blocks without global compaction; 3) attach lightweight allocation metadata to entries to allow opportunistic relocation during low-load windows; 4) expose a fragmentation hint to the continuous batching controller so it can avoid request groupings that would cause large non-contiguous allocations. This optimizes for the common-case streaming inference (small allocation increments, long-lived KV for prefixes) while providing graceful background healing when idle.
implementation_steps: Design in-memory layout: micro-segment descriptor (8B), segment affinity tags, and epoch counters
Add reservoir pool manager: APIs for checkout/checkin micro-segments with LRU aging
Implement sliding-window allocator: hot-window ring per GPU with fast-path allocation and fallback to reservoir
Batching controller integration: fragmentation hint protocol and soft placement policy
Background relocation worker: low-priority compaction that merges adjacent micro-segments into slabs during idle cycles
Telemetry: fragmentation score, reservoir hit-rate, relocation throughput, and latency impact
End-to-end soak test and safety checks (OOM guardrails, relocation timeouts)
rollout_plan: 1) Feature gated behind runtime flag; 2) Canary on internal sandbox with synthetic high-variance sequence-length workloads (3 days); 3) Beta on 10% of traffic with verbose telemetry; 4) Measure metrics for 72h and tune window sizes; 5) Gradual ramp to 100% with automated rollback on SLO regressions.
telemetry_and_metrics: fragmentation_score: ratio of free segments to largest-contiguous-free-block
reservoir_hit_rate: percent allocations satisfied by reservoir without global alloc
acceptance_criteria: Reservoir hit rate >= 65% on synthetic mixed-batch workload
Fragmentation score improved by >= 40% vs baseline after 24h of mixed traffic
No increase in p99 token latency > 5% during normal traffic in canary
Relocation worker limited to <= 5% of device bandwidth and CPU budget
Automated rollback triggers on OOM spike or p99 latency regression
tasks: Spec review with infra and runtime teams
Proto implement allocator and reservoir manager
Add relocation worker and idle-detection heuristics
Run large-scale soak and collect results
risks_and_mitigation: Risk: Relocation can steal GPU cycles -> Mitigation: enforce strict QoS and throttle by GPU util and token throughput
Risk: Reservoir fragmentation itself grows -> Mitigation: periodic reservoir compaction with epoch-based reclamation
Risk: Incorrect batching hints degrade throughput -> Mitigation: fall back to default placement and monitor throughput metrics
Risk: Edge cases with very large sequences causing long contiguous allocation needs -> Mitigation: reserve a small emergency contiguous slab pool and expose metric for operators

notes: This approach prioritizes low-latency steady-state inference by avoiding heavy, synchronous compaction. If successful it becomes the default allocator for GPUs running continuous batching workloads; fallback remains the existing slab allocator to ensure safety during rollout. Close collaboration with the batching team is required to tune placement hints so we don't inadvertently create allocation anti-patterns.
